extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, jurists, lawyers, and policymakers interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical exposition of the political effects of the legal profession and the institution of trial by jury on democratic republics, especially the United States. Discusses causes that maintain democracy and the social/political role of lawyers and juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawyers' attachment to public order and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawyers are attached to public order beyond every other consideration, and the best security of public order is authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They value the legality of institutions far more than their freedom; they are less afraid of tyranny than of arbitrary power. This predisposes them to favor stability and legal formality over popular independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchs can co-opt legal practitioners as instruments of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A monarch will always be able to convert legal practitioners into the most serviceable instruments of his authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because lawyers have greater affinity with executive power than with the people, entrusting them with despotic power tends to make that power assume external features of justice and legality. A ruler diminishing judicial authority or the influence of lawyers would often lose substance for a shadow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawyers as connecting link between people and aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawyers belong to the people by birth and interest, to the aristocracy by habit and by taste, and may be looked upon as the natural bond and connecting link of the two great classes of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their mixed affinities allow them to mediate between classes and to divert democracy from its natural tendencies through means foreign to its nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: The legal profession as the sole aristocratic element compatible with democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession of the law is the only aristocratic element which can be amalgamated without violence with the natural elements of democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite defects in lawyers' character, their sober, law-focused influence is necessary to maintain democratic institutions; a republic might not subsist without increasing legal influence proportionate to popular power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent-based legal systems foster reverence for the old and conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: English and American lawyers have retained the law of precedents; in their minds a taste and a reverence for what is old is almost always united to a love of regular and lawful proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subjection of thought and implicit deference to forefathers engenders timid habits and sluggish inclinations, making legal change difficult and promoting conservatism in civil law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law practitioners emphasize precedents; civil-law advocates emphasize reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The English and Americans investigate what has been done; the French advocate inquires what should have been done; the former produce precedents, the latter reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In common-law countries lawyers frequently quote others' opinions and defer to precedent; in civil-law countries litigation often involves disputing fundamental principles. This affects how law is practiced and how accessible it is to the uninitiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law complexity makes legal knowledge inaccessible and elevates the profession
rubrics_metrics.description: The indispensable want of legal assistance felt in England and the United States and the high opinion of the profession tend to separate it more and more from the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation founded on precedents can be impenetrable to the uninitiated; the common-law lawyer resembles a hierophant and becomes the sole interpreter of an occult science, raising the social station of lawyers and distancing them from lay society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social position of lawyers shapes their political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: In English society lawyers constitute, as it were, the younger branch of the English aristocracy; in America lawyers form the highest political class and the most cultivated circle of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their station causes them to absorb aristocratic tastes and to exercise conservative influence; in the United States they are often the principal counterpoise to the democratic element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal profession as counterpoise to democratic excesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal profession forms the most powerful, if not the only, counterpoise to the democratic element in America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawyers neutralize vices inherent in popular government by opposing aristocratic propensities to democratic instincts, reverence for the antique to love of novelty, narrow views to immense designs, and procrastination to impatience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts and judges as visible organs controlling democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts of justice are the most visible organs by which the legal profession is enabled to control the democracy. The judge, armed with the power of declaring the laws to be unconstitutional, perpetually interferes in political affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges can't force lawmaking but can prevent the people from acting inconsistently with their own enactments. Innovations like elective judges or legislative removal are predicted to be dangerous to judicial independence and to the republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawyers' dominance in public office shapes legislation and resists civil-law innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: As lawyers constitute the only enlightened class which the people does not mistrust, they are naturally called upon to occupy most public stations; they fill legislative assemblies and conduct the administration, exercising powerful influence upon law formation and execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because majorities defer to legal authority in civil law matters, Americans have introduced many political innovations but made very sparing alterations in civil laws, which are often repugnant to social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury as a political institution that embodies sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: By the jury I mean a certain number of citizens chosen indiscriminately, and invested with a temporary right of judging; the jury is pre-eminently a political institution and must be regarded as one form of the sovereignty of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen politically, the jury places the direction of society in the hands of the governed (or a portion of them) rather than the government; it can be aristocratic or democratic depending on which class supplies jurors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury composition should track the franchise (elector list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of citizens qualified to serve on juries must increase and diminish with the list of electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators should align jury qualifications with suffrage to preserve consistency of popular sovereignty; treating jury qualification solely as a question of intelligence misses the political nature of the institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of jury to civil causes increases its political and civic influence
rubrics_metrics.description: When the influence of the jury is extended to civil causes its application is constantly palpable; it affects all the interests of the community and fashions the human mind to its peculiar forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil juries penetrate daily life, associate the idea of justice with popular participation, and are harder to remove than juries confined to criminal causes; civil jury use is a strong foundation for free institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury as education: practical public school of citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury contributes most powerfully to form the judgement and to increase the natural intelligence of a people; it may be regarded as a gratuitous public school ever open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every juror learns to exercise rights, engages with learned members of society, becomes acquainted with laws through bar and judge, and this experience is a chief source of practical intelligence and political good sense in democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury in civil cases consolidates judicial authority and transmits legal spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: In civil causes the judge appears as a disinterested arbiter and his influence upon verdict is almost unlimited; the jury sanctions the decision of the judge by society's authority while he contributes reason and law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although jury seems to restrict magistracy, it consolidates judges' power: judges gain authority from civil jury experience and continue to influence society beyond the courtroom, both socially and politically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic republic maintained by three principal heads
rubrics_metrics.description: All the causes which contribute to the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States are reducible to three heads: (I) The peculiar and accidental situation in which Providence has placed the Americans; (II) The laws; (III) The manners and customs of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a classificatory rubric for analyzing why American democracy endures; the chapter proceeds to enumerate accidental/providential causes in support of head I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of dangerous neighbors reduces need for military glory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have no neighbors — consequently they have no great wars, financial crises, inroads, or conquest to dread; they require neither great taxes, nor great armies, nor great generals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of external threats prevents the ascent of military glory, which Tocqueville sees as a corrosive force for republics (example: Jackson's election influenced by past military victory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of a single dominant metropolis preserves republicanism
rubrics_metrics.description: America has no great capital city whose influence is felt over the whole country; the absence of a metropolis is one of the first causes of the maintenance of republican institutions in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large cities act as assemblies that can concert and rouse populace influence on magistrates; a dominant metropolis concentrates power and threatens representative systems. Urban masses and corrupt local governments in large cities are noted as dangers.
